Sean Ahlquist
Abstract
As the knowledge of material computation advances, continuing the seamless integration of design and fabrication,
questions beyond materialization can be addressed with a focus on sensing, feedback, and engagement as critical factors
of design exploration. This article will discuss a series of prototypes, design methodologies, and technologies that
articulate a textile’s micro-architecture, at the scale of fibers and stitches, to instrumentalize simultaneous structural,
spatial, and sensory-responsive qualities. The progression of research displays an ever-deepening instrumentalization of
fiber structure and its implications to form definition and responsivity, in creating form- and bending-active structures.
The research results in a more refined definition of material behavior as the innate phenomena which emerge at
the moment of textile fabrication. Ultimately, the architecture, in its materiality and physical, visual, and auditory
responsivity, is designed to address specific challenges for children in filtering multiple sensory inputs, an underlying
factor of autism spectrum disorder.
Keywords
CNC Knitting, Form-active, Bending-active, Textile hybrid, Mutli-sensory
Introduction
This article presents new research in textile-based structures to imagine an architecture for tactile and spatial
engagement. Architecture, in this research, serves as the interface for human–computer interaction.
Intelligence is embedded in the responsiveness of the architecture to enhance the user’s comprehension of
their multi-sensory experience in time and space, which is addressed primarily in designing and calibrating
the quality of deformability from the scale of the hand to the body, and coordinating the movement of both.
The formation of architecture is the realization of its material composition as a structural system that con-
tinually deforms as the hand and body reshape it to create a coherent sensory spatial state.

Material composition, in the research described here, is formed by a textile-based structural system,
referred to as a textile hybrid. Form is realized at the equilibrium of more than one type of structural action,
invoking the term hybrid as defined by Heino Engel1 in the classification of fundamental structural systems.
Specifically, the integration of tensile (form-active) surfaces and linear networks of actively bent (bending-
active) composite beams comprises the lightweight self-stable textile hybrid system.2–4 This article presents
the exploration of knitted textiles as a unique facet in both the form-active and bending-active capacities of
the system. Through advancements in both aspects, the structural system is able to address simultaneously
the multi-scalar features of engagement from touch and pressure at the application of the hand, to the balanc-
ing of deflection and support at the scale and movement of the body throughout the architecture.
In this research, coherency of one’s temporal spatial experience is defined by an understanding of sensory
processing. More specifically, the architectures being developed address challenges which face individuals whose
capacities for sensory processing are diminished. This is referred to as Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD), a
condition where a “traffic jam” of unfiltered, unrestrained sensory data leads to an over-intensified experience of
space and all of its sensory features. Such a dysregulated state may occur through either over-responsivity or
under-responsivity to the visual, auditory, and physical. Critically, this affects the ability for self-regulation, motor
control, and, ultimately, learning and interaction with others.5 This research contributes a unique design approach
by developing tactile and spatial descriptions whose focus is not to correct sensory malfunction but rather supply
the level of filtered responsivity that sorts and regulates the multi-sensory experience.
A series of prototypes are described in this article to show the development of material and structural
strategies which allow for tailoring the multi-sensory temporal and spatial experience to individuals which
have over- or under-responsive sensory systems. Through a prototype titled Semi-toroidal Textile Hybrid,
the textile is transformed into a highly heterogeneous structure, through the use of Computer Numerical
Controlled (CNC) knitting, where the qualities of the fiber and the manipulation of knit structure are utilized
to satisfy structural needs and explore spatial qualities. Exploring more closely the relationship to knit struc-
ture and the distribution of tensile forces, the Mobius Rib-knit Textile Hybrid prototype advances the ability
to express tactility through realizing a highly undulating surface in pure tension and in balance with the
bending-active boundary. Advancing both the spatial description and structural capacity of the architectural
system, a more expansive spatial and multi-sensory experience is explored with the StretchPLAY prototype
which activates a visual, physical, and auditory responsiveness, directly addressing the challenges surround-
ing SPD (Figure 1).
Figure 1. StretchPLAY textile hybrid prototype activates the architecture as a multi-sensory, responsive playscape.

Expanded morphospaces of architecture
The concept of a material system encapsulates the inextricable relationship between material and form,
based on processes of fabrication and assembly, and the repercussive performative effects in response to
contextual forces and energies.6 This is a systems-centric approach where the definition of a specific material
system is produced by a series of integrated morphological processes. In this research, the spectrum of both
material and environmental processes is greatly expanded, proposing an ecomorphological view of material
systems. Form, as a macrocosm of minute multi-hierarchical material behaviors, is a temporal condition in
fluctuation via the charge of internal and external energies, as part of a socio-spatial sensory architecture.
Morphology is a term defined by Geothe7 to describe the generation of structured form and its continual
transformation as a biological organism within an ecosystem. Mapping of the morphological parameters for
material, ecology, and time provides the definition of a morphospace, a multi-axial graph which houses the
descriptions of forms both real and possible.8 In biology, this is referred to as a theoretical morphospace. In
design, this is an elaboration of the parametric design space. Achim Menges depicts the necessity for this
approach, establishing a machinic morphospace in order to understand the design space which bounds form
generation within the possibilities for robotic prefabrication. This generates a non-hierarchical view of the
parametric design space, where materialization is not a derivative of shape generation. Rather, the mor-
phospace is a thorough mapping of the parameters and their relationships which underlie potential mor-
phologies within the constraints of materialization.9 The following begins to disentangle the axes of a
morphospace intending to map the relationships between the material behavior of textiles, the system behav-
ior of textile hybrid structures, and the factors that necessitate a responsive sensory-engaged architecture.
Material capacities and tendencies
Manuel DeLanda articulates the relationship between material and system behavior through the definition of
properties, tendencies, and capacities. Properties are the immutable material characteristics in isolation of
external influence—a specific state, while tendencies and capacities are defined by interaction—a specific
event involving an effector.10 Parsing the latter as nuances of system behavior, tendencies are events where
the system itself is the effector, while capacities elicit a new event, an action which subsequently transforms
the very systems involved. Tendencies are multivalent yet, based upon the properties of the system, they are
finite in reaching a particular state. Capacities are more complexly measurable as interaction involves
describing the nature of an imposition involving another unique set of material and system behaviors.
Working in the realm of fibrous structures, in textiles and fiber-reinforced composite materials, the material
system is formed of processes which span a wide range of scales. Properties themselves are defined by interac-
tions, fibers being oriented, being bonded, taking on the nature of a capacity. The relationship from properties
to material and system behavior is multi-hierarchical; the tendencies and capacities defined by a specific prop-
erty at one scale will help shape the properties at a subsequent scale. The material system becomes a morpho-
genetic description, a fluid intermingling of properties and material formation.11 This is exemplified, in this
research, by the continuous layering of material behavior from the properties of a fiber to the tendencies of
interacting fibers and ultimately the capacities of a form- and bending-active structural system. Capacities
enmesh the system of a textile hybrid and its geometric material transformation at the moment of physical
engagement. The resulting event is the significantly individualized definition of a spatial sensory experience.
Multimodal experience of architecture
In the experience of space and time, perception is formed by the seamless integration of initially segregated
multimodal (multi-sensory) data, where perception provides the foundation for a coordinated and appropri-
ate response to the complex array of both internal and external, social and non-social stimuli.12 To achieve

66 International Journal of Architectural Computing 14(1)
the appropriate response through an interface, referred to as human–computer interaction, is a function of
selecting which modalities are activated and the intuitive manner of how they are combined. Increased cali-
bration between the multimodal stimuli fosters a more natural and persuasive experience.13 This entails
knowledge of the innate patterns of an individual’s sensory system to combine multimodal stimuli, and their
resulting perception of the spatial temporal experience.14
In this research, the tactile sense is the primary focus in how the related stimuli integrate with information
from other senses (visual and auditory) to define perception, experience, and interaction with an architecture.
The sense of touch is defined by mechanoreceptors distributed in various densities throughout the body,
from the skin to muscles and joints. Information for tactile perception is captured in the layers of the skin,
while interaction with objects and the environment, kinesthesia, is defined by receptors embedded in the
muscles and joints. It is the combined processing of such multimodal data of touch and movement in the
somatosensory system that produces the understanding of position and relation of body and limbs in space.15
Referred to as proprioception, the comprehension of position in space additionally involves the vestibular
system: the perception of balance, orientation, and degrees of motion. As the foundation for experience
within physical space, the vestibular information is formed by stimulation of various mechanoreceptors in
the inner ear. The processing of proper vestibular input prepares the entire nervous system to receive and
respond to other sensations effectively and appropriately.16
The aspect of SPD which this research addresses is hyporesponsivity where a behavioral response is either
lacking or muted in reaction to sensory stimuli, such as lacking orientation toward sounds or recognition of pain.
An inability to register input from novel social or non-social stimuli causes an individual to miss learning oppor-
tunities and prevent development for foundational skills of social communication, a key facet especially for
children where significant learning takes place through interaction with others.17 In children with autism, repeti-
tive behaviors and impairments in communication, language skills, and social interaction have been linked to
high degrees of hyporesponsivity.18,19 In particular, the research focuses on dysfunction in the sense of touch and
the vestibular system, where the understanding of tactility, body awareness, movement, and balance are dimin-
ished. Disorder in the sense of touch disturbs motor planning, the ability to move with purpose and ease, along
with visual discrimination and language, as touch is a critical feature in associating words with actions and
objects.20 Vestibular dysfunction elicits awkward and uncoordinated movements, where a particular sensory
seeking behavior involves increased desire for vigorous movement, all leading to physical over-activity, poor
balance, auditory processing (poor vestibular receptors in the inner ear), and emotional insecurity.20
Sensory Integration, practiced by an occupational therapist, is an approach which seeks to develop inter-
ventions combining the vestibular, proprioceptive, and tactile sensations.21 To provide enhanced tactile sen-
sation, modalities are founded on the use of deep pressure and activities involving the proprioceptive sense.
This ranges in scale from applying pressure, massage, or vibration on joints, to a cloth swing, and using
resistive equipment for jumping, pushing, and pulling. In utilizing these methods, a critical factor is the
interplay between the intensity, frequency, duration, and rhythm.22 The benefit of a particular intervention
can be measured by modulating such interplay, looking for improved alertness, organized behavior, and
reduced signs of stress, sensory defensiveness, and hyperactivity.
Differentiated textile hybrid material systems
The specific classification of a textile hybrid emphasizes the priority of the fibrous composition of the
bending-active elements and of the textile membranes in forming an integrated architecture. The term “bend-
ing-active” refers to beams which have been elastically deformed, gaining stiffness through geometry and
residual stress, most suitably accomplished with high strength fiber-reinforced materials with low bending
stiffness.2 Regarding the form-active textile, central to this research is the shift from a bi-axial fiber uniform-
ity, of an often used woven textile, to one of a variegated fiber organization. The exploration of

Ahlquist 67
differentiation takes place through the use of CNC weft-knitting, where knit structure is designed in response
to form-active pre-stress and to realize particular tactile spatial qualities.
A material system can be broken down into three primary characteristics: topology, structural action, and
materiality, serving as the decoupled variables and constraints for design exploration of the fully integrated
system.23 In a textile hybrid, topology defines the number, type, and manners of association between the
textile and composite rod elements. Structural action refers to the application of form- and bending-active
stresses to the network of elements. Materiality encapsulates the properties which underlie the element
types, as well as the logics which define system assembly. In this research, these parameters operate in a
multi-scalar hierarchical fashion as the formation of a knitted textile incurs the logic of a material system
within itself. The act of knitting instigates a material behavior as the inter-looping of fibers activates stresses
and geometries based upon relationships between material properties and individual stitch structures. This
signifies an important shift from the manipulation of standardized materials to explicit production of graded
materials, highly tailored for their performative value.24
Form-finding structural behavior
To resolve material behaviors driven by both tensile and bending stiffness, this research focuses on the use
of spring-based numerical methods, intimately coordinated with form-finding efforts through physical
experimentation and finite element analysis.2,25 The programming of spring-based methods utilizes particle
systems, consisting of particles defining mass and position, and springs defining axial stiffness whose calcu-
lation of force exertion follows Hooke’s Law of Elasticity.26,27 Particular material behaviors are defined
through spring topologies placed as positional constraints on the particles of variable (user-defined) net-
works of springs. A hierarchy is established where certain springs serve to provide force characteristics of
tension, compression, or bending stiffness, while other particle-spring networks define meshes representa-
tive of a physical geometry. At any level of the system, though, all elements exert force of certain intensity
along a particular vector. The mechanical behavior for bending stiffness is approximated in particular topo-
logical arrangements of springs applied to the nodes along a linear array of particle-springs. Three primary
numerical methods have been established in Computer Graphics: cross-over, vertex position, and vertex
normal, simulating bending behavior of elements assumed to have a continuous material description and
cross-section.28 The vertex normal method is used to simulate three degrees of freedom, involving a value
for Young’s Modulus allowing a more accurate simulation of specific materials and cross-sections.29
Spring-based methods rely primarily upon relative descriptions of force characteristics enabling explora-
tions of textile hybrids to advance in complexity, specification, and form through efficient computation, and
without explicit material definition. Springs are utilized to negotiate the relationships between tensile stresses
and bending-active force by simulating stiffness. Each spring, or collection of springs which define a nodal
stiffness, provides means to explore heterogeneity in the system. In cases where the complexity in the rela-
tionships of the textile hybrid belies intuition, iterative feedback through the computational environment
elicits knowledge in particular topological and behavioral manipulations.23 Such is the focus of the modeling
environment springFORM, programmed in Processing (Java) by the author, and utilized in developing the
range of textile hybrid systems outlined in this article.
Semi-toroidal prototype
The Semi-toroidal Textile Hybrid prototype (Figure 2) tempers the stretch of a highly elastic poly-elastan yarn
with stitch structures that vary to accomplish both pattern and differential form-active stresses.23 Cast-off, or
“dropped,” stitches maximize the scale of the stitch at the boundaries of the textile, allowing it to expand up to
2.7 times its manufactured circumference to meet the geometry of the bending-active frame. The cast-off stitch

Figure 2. Semi-toroidal textile hybrid prototype greatly varies stitch structure to capture high ranges of elasticity in
expressing a distorted hexagonal structure (left) and moments of compression within the textile (right).
is utilized in the field of the textile, as well, to enhance the visual and structural contrast to the “all-needle”
structure of the hexagonal pattern. Increased stitch density, in both the field and hexagonal structures, produces
a self-forming of the textile, where shape is maintained at moments of minimal stress. The compact stitch den-
sity embeds a compressive capacity, especially in the hexagonal patterning, where the textile can form its own
geometric features when the external imposed form-active stress is minimized. This vast range of active and
embedded textile properties are encapsulated within an architecture comprising only a single bending-active
boundary, a seamless textile cylinder, and a four-sided textile panel (Figure 3).
Mobius Rib-knit prototype
Exploring the fundamental nature of machine knitting, the Mobius Rib-knit Textile Hybrid prototype exhib-
its the play between the material behavior at the scale of the stitch, and system behavior in the response of
the textile to imposed tensile forces (Figure 4). The prototype exploits a rib-knit structure, whose fundamen-
tally elastic nature emerges from the differentiation between stitches formed on either the front or back
needle bed on a weft-knitting machine. A weighted bias is produced with stitches formed on a single needle
bed, which drives the resulting textile to naturally “recoil.” The relationship of the head of one stitch to the
legs of the successive stitch determines that direction of recoil, while the yarn properties and stitch length
define the magnitude of the rebounding quality (Figure 5). Alternating stitches from the front and back nee-
dle bed produces a series of neighboring ribs, commonly used as cuffs and collars of sweaters providing
great ranges of elasticity without the need for an elastic yarn, which can quickly fatigue.
By gaining elasticity with the rib-knit logic, the prototype is formed of a relatively inelastic yarn, an air-
jet textured polyester yarn, in combination with varying the dimension and number of ribs, providing the
means to tailor the textile to the system behavior of the form- and bending-active prototype. Data in the

dimensionality of the tensile surface and the ratio of tensile stresses are derived from a spring-based simula-
tion using the java-based software springFORM (Figure 6). The analysis of these parameters deals with the
following rules: (1) if the ratio is weighted toward the latitudinal direction of the mesh, a parallel-running

In the Semi-Toroidal prototype, the lowest level of resolution explored is that of the hexagonal region;
determining the number of rows and columns of hexagonal cells was the most refined level of articulating
the textile. In contrast, the operable level of resolution for the Mobius Rib-knit prototype is at both the scale
of the rib as a non-uniform structure and the stitch as the ultimate parameter for controlling both elastic
behavior and overall textile shape. Operating at such a scale of material formation and behavior, the overall
system produces a visual and spatial complexity and operates as an undulating tactile surface, a highly
unique quality in the field of pre-stressed lightweight structures.
Materialization, responsivity, and system behavior
The StretchPLAY prototype, as a part of the Social Sensory Surfaces research project, integrates the abil-
ity to produce and tune tactile qualities of a topologically complex textile hybrid system for the purpose

lenges in sensory processing is studied to provide a specific understanding of the relation between sen-

field of therapies for SPD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The project addresses issues of sensory
processing where the nervous system is unable to filter sensory input in order to determine an appropriate
response, leading to physical, social, and behavioral challenges. To counteract this “traffic jam” of sen-
sory data, the prototype promotes a sensory regulating environment by acutely tailoring the relationship
between scale, material elasticity, structural deformation, and visual, physical, and auditory feedback.
This involves the advancement of the structural robustness of a textile hybrid system, and the implemen-
tation of the textile as a tangible, sensing interface, activating the entire system as a dynamically respon-
sive multimodal playscape.

A single child is studied, a 5-year-old girl, to utilize the manner in which she engages her environment, as
a spatial, social, sensory experience, as the backbone for explorations in the design of the structure and inter-
actions with it. The intent is to cater to the child’s sensory needs, to produce a regulated, focused state, at
which point challenges in social engagement and collaborative play could be addressed. The child being
studied has ASD and sensory challenges which place her in the realm of under-responsivity to sensory
stimuli, producing challenges in fine and gross motor control, verbal communication, behavioral regulation,
and social interaction. A range of methods are employed to develop a sensory and behavioral profile.
Dynamics for social interaction is derived through playtime interactions between the child and students and
researchers involved in the project. As the child is non-verbal, information is gleaned through close exami-
nation of movement, gestures, and facial expressions. More concise descriptions of her interests and limita-
tions in fine/gross motor activities, task-related efforts, and back-and-forth communication are defined
respectively by input from therapists in occupational therapy (OT), applied behavioral analysis (ABA), and
the Play and Language for Autistic Youngsters (PLAY) Project, who have worked with the child on a regular
basis.
Spatial playscape
The complexity in form, material behavior, and system behavior arises from the manner by which the rod
structure and textile associate individually and collectively. The Semi-toroidal prototype expresses a clarity
in form through the use of a seamless cylindrical textile. The visual and spatial complexity of the Mobius
Rib-knit prototype is achieved through the inter-looping of the bending-active Glass Fiber Reinforced Polymer
(GFRP) boundary and a four-sided textile panel. The StretchPLAY prototype combines both capacities,
advancing the topological complexity of the seamless textile and the interconnectedness of the GFRP bound-
ary (Figure 7).
The spatial organization encompasses a range of scales and directional movements. Cued from the child’s
interaction with spaces of various scales, those of a size where she could touch and closely identify all sur-
faces around her leading to more regulated states where clear communication and desire for social interac-
tion was observed. Smaller spaces can better organize the proprioceptive sense and provide calming.30
Allowing active touch and close proximity with all surrounding surfaces overcomes the loss of the ability for
signals from the inner ear to indicate position, orientation in space, and relationship of the limbs to the body.
Seamless knitted textile
The textile component of the StretchPLAY prototype advances upon the techniques for structure, materiality,
and form established with the Semi-toroidal prototype. The textile is formed of a highly elastic yarn compris-
ing a Spandex core with a stretch-nylon cover, often referred to as “nylastic.” Initial scale studies are used to
explore the spatial organization and develop a knit logic which allows the entire structure to be formed of a
single seamless textile (Figure 8). In the Semi-toroidal prototype, a “cast-off” stitch is utilized to produce
maximum stretchability as well as means to visually express the “all-needle” structure of the meta-scale
hexagonal pattern. In contrast, the StretchPLAY prototype confines the cast-off stitch to only a few courses
at the boundary, utilizing the all-needle structure, with varied stitch length, to create a dense and highly
resilient textile when in tension as a part of the textile hybrid system. The previous textile hybrid prototypes
dealt only will the internal stresses related to the negotiation of form- and bending-active forces. StretchPLAY
responds to the significant shift of utilizing the structure as an engaged playscape, dealing with the imposi-
tion of force from the scale of the hand to the body.
As with the Semi-toroidal prototype, the all-needle structure aids in managing reduced lateral stresses in
the tubes at the front and back of the structures. Typical to a tensioned cylinder and evident in the

CNC knitting machine, M1 Plus (Figure 9).
Multi-hierarchical bending-active laminated beam construction
A challenge with the bending-active component of a textile hybrid system is the ability to vary and articulate
the geometry within a single structure. Working with varying GFRP cross-sections within a single system is
difficult as the end-to-end connections between rods are problematic both materially and structurally. In
contrast, working with a single cross-section limits the range of radii that can be accomplished. Ideally, the
radii want to meet a geometry and permissible tensile stress to create a stable structural state, with a minimal
amount of variation from the ideal condition. Equation (1) provides the means to calculate the minimal

bending radius for a particular material description with a round cross-section, where the tensile strength is
calculated at 80% of the material’s limit. The necessity to withstand more significant point loads through a
child climbing on the structure additionally poses a challenge in structuring the desired geometry. To gain
more stiffness without reducing span, a larger GFRP cross-section is necessary. Yet, a larger GFRP cross-
section cannot accomplish the tight and varied radii defined by the form-finding process. As a result, a new
method of fabrication is developed into order to provide a robust structure to accomplish the scale and geom-
etry as defined by the design process.

The design of the StretchPLAY architecture takes advantage of springFORM’s ability to manipulate only
the negotiation of form- and bending-active forces. This allows for a freedom in form-finding reflective of
structural action over constraints of specific material definition. Manipulating properties by node, rather than
by entire linear element or mesh, allows for highly heterogeneous forms to be produced. As a result, the
bending-active component of the StretchPLAY prototype comprises radii which span from 30 to 100 inches
(Figure 10). Based upon the use of equation (1), a 0.5-inch diameter GFRP rod is appropriate for an approx.
30-inch bending radius, while a rod cross-section of 1.6 inches is necessary to accomplish a properly struc-
tured 100-inch bending radius. As mentioned previously, such geometric variation cannot be accomplished

76 International Journal of Architectural Computing 14(1)
Figure 11. A knitted sleeve is used to bundle 0.5-inch diameter rods, which are subsequently form-found into the
full-scale geometry and resin impregnated through vacuum-forming to create a laminated beam.
through the interconnection of rods with differing cross-sections. In response, a method of bundling and
lamination of small cross-section GFRP tubes is developed to accomplish a range of radii within a single
continuous system, while producing a robust construction, able to take loading beyond self-weight and inter-
nal stresses.
For the prototype, three 0.5-inch diameter GFRP rods are bundled into a custom knitted sleeve that seam-
lessly connects separate channels for each of the rods. By bundling the rods and allowing for shear move-
ment between them, the structure can be form-found to match the minimal bending radius allowable by a
single GFRP rod. To develop a more robust beam condition, the knitted sleeve is impregnated in-situ with
epoxy resin and vacuum-formed, creating a bond between the rods and removing the possibility for shear
(Figure 11). Additionally, secondary GFRP rods are inserted to stabilize pivot points within the rod topology.
Using fixed mechanical connections can cause peak stresses and failure at the interface between the rod and
the connector. In this case, by using a consistent material type, the structure realizes a more fluid elasticity.
With this multi-hierarchical system of GFRP rods and laminated GFRP beams, finite element analysis shows
the ability to resist a significant point load with minimal deflection (Table 1 and Figure 12).
Pressure-sensitive and spatial interaction design
As a framework for interaction with the textile architecture, this research employs an approach involving
individualized, family-inclusive, and socially oriented play. The PLAY Project and Early Social Interaction
(ESI) are two early-intervention therapies that stress one-on-one engagement with children in their natural
environment, parent training, and parent involvement in therapy. Both focus on a variety of social impair-
ments, centering on observation and responsiveness to the child’s specific needs as they change from moment
to moment.31,32 The PLAY project, a collaborator in the development of the StretchPLAY prototype, addresses
social impairments by following and responding to the child’s lead in play-based activities. The PLAY pro-
ject uses six markers, referred to as Functional Developmental Levels (FDL), to assess individual strengths
and challenges in the realm of social interaction: (1) self-regulation and shared attention, (2) engagement, (3)
two-way communication, (4) complex two-way communication, (5) shared meanings and symbolic play,
and (6) emotional thinking. By repeated reinforcements of back-and-forth communication through the means
of play, social interaction can be built as a more innate response, where for children with behavioral issues
related to sensory processing, this type of interaction is unsettling and not instinctive.

The StretchPLAY prototype is centered on FDL 1–3, fostering self-regulation as the first step in generat-
ing social engagement and simple back-and-forth communication. The landscape of the textile is set with a
series of triggers, sensed by a Microsoft Kinect to identify when the textile has been pressed to a certain

78 International Journal of Architectural Computing 14(1)
Figure 13. Trigger points are dispersed through the structure based upon a 10 × 10 grid defined in the gaming
software Unity.
depth at such a location (Figure 13). The trigger points, laid out within a 10 by 10 grid, are initially hidden
in order to encourage extended movement and tactile sensation by traversing across the surface. Once a trig-
ger is found, the following steps are initiated: (1) a circle pulses to help reinforce memory of where the
activation point is, (2) followed by the projection of an animation across the surface of the textile, and (3)
playing of a sound clip synchronized with the contents of the animation.
The effort of finding trigger points ensures both an aspect of exploration, but also guarantees gross
motor movement as a part of the playing process. The quality of resistance in pushing on the tensioned
textile is an important feature in registering the sense of touch. With difficulties in sensory processing, a
strong resistance applies pressure to the joints not just the hand and finger tips, giving a better chance for
the tactility to be identified as well as providing a calming effect. Certain animations play only when two
triggers are simultaneously activated. Once the logic of finding and activating a single trigger to produce
the visual and auditory feedback becomes familiar, the social component can be unfolded encouraging
cooperation of two individuals to activate the paired triggers. The gaming engine Unity processes the tex-
tile interactions, while the software MadMapper is used to transform and re-orient the animations for pro-
jection onto the surface of the structure (Figure 14).
Conclusion
The material, physical, visual, and auditory responsivity of the StretchPLAY prototype, as shown in Figure
15, is designed to address specific challenges for children in filtering multiple sensory inputs, an underlying
aspect of ASD. The play experience itself is intended to be extremely straightforward. This is to foster a state

of sensory regulation and a sense of control over the quality of the space which is being occupied. Ultimately,
this is in service of the primary goal of play as the means for embedding social interaction as a regular,
expected, and comfortable part of the experience. In the case of the child being studied in this project, due to
her non-verbal nature, communication has to be established through means alternative to speaking. Play, in
this context, is oriented to both discover the means of communication and also reinforce them

through repetitive, positive, and successful experiences. Where the research described in this article is
focused primarily on the technological development of responsivity in textile structures, further research
looks to examine play, through the engagement with such architectures, to measure the development of the
social skills of children with autism and underlying sensory challenges.
This research traverses many fields and concepts to lay a framework for the conceptualization, design,
and application of materially complex and dynamically responsive architectural systems. In the defini-
tion of calm technology, the periphery is a pivotal concept in recognizing that which is critical but lies
just beyond our center of focus. A calm technology allows the periphery to shift forward and back with
ease, and without distraction.33 Additionally, the expansiveness of the term form, to include the act of
engagement, deformation, and sensory transformation, adopts a virtual morphology, or an “anorganic
vitality … unformed, indeterminate, loose enough that other figuration, other confabulations may yet
happen in it or pass through it.”34
